_note: Exposure Pathway scores, 1 (low) to 3 (high). Iteration 3 scores are Claude's judgement from the verified evidence, for the author to review. Each score has a one-line note; 'sources' lists the evidence behind the row.

dimensions.label: Harm severity
dimensions.question: How serious are documented abuses at the source?

dimensions.label: Evidence strength
dimensions.question: Is the link to fusion proven (3), likely (2), or hypothetical (1)?

dimensions.label: Traceability break
dimensions.question: Is there a blending point where origin is lost?

dimensions.label: Fusion leverage
dimensions.question: Inverted: 3 = least leverage. Can fusion buyers alone change anything, or only by pooling with other sectors?

notes.harm: Child miners' deaths, violence and sexual exploitation of workers, deadly landslides, armed-group control.
notes.evidence: Chinese customs data show 28,000+ t of rare earths from Myanmar in Jan–Sep 2025, but no record traces any of it into tape.
notes.traceability: Ore is mixed into Chinese separation plants and leaves as Chinese product.
notes.leverage: Fusion is now a main customer of HTS tape makers, but has no leverage over separators or mines alone.

notes.harm: Severe environmental damage (US$5.6bn cleanup, 50–100 years to recover); no documented abuses against people.
notes.evidence: China produces most of the world's yttrium, so fusion yttrium likely includes it; no record shows it.
notes.traceability: Country of origin survives, but specific mines are lost at separation.
notes.leverage: Same as Kachin: leverage over tape makers, not over Chinese separators.

notes.harm: Controlled by a US-sanctioned armed group listed by the UN for child recruitment; 2022 explosion killed nine.
notes.evidence: Yunnan Tin told Reuters some of its tin came from the Wa mine, and Bruker's group smelter list names Yunnan Tin; the link into strand is likely, not proven.
notes.traceability: No smelters in Wa; ore is smelted in Yunnan and no trade records show the flow.
notes.leverage: Fusion's tin demand is tiny next to electronics solder; only a cross-sector pool could move it.

routes.label: Tin
routes.route: Great Lakes traders → Malaysia Smelting Corp

notes.harm: Smelter bought ore from an OFAC-sanctioned trader tied to Rubaya; harm is at the source, the link is indirect.
notes.evidence: Nothing shows this smelter's tin reaching a fusion strand maker.
notes.traceability: Records name countries, not mines; Rwandan exports mix in smuggled Congolese ore.
notes.leverage: Same as Wa State: fusion is a negligible tin buyer.

notes.harm: Forced labour, torture and killings of miners by M23; mass deaths in tunnel collapses.
notes.evidence: Brazil supplies about 93% of niobium; no record links Rubaya coltan to a strand maker.
notes.traceability: Laundered as 'Rwandan' exports and processed by smelters that passed audits.
notes.leverage: Superconductor niobium is a sliver of a market dominated by steelmaking.

notes.harm: Legacy barium contamination under a prosecutors' agreement; no reports of conflict, forced or child labour.
notes.evidence: Western Superconducting's prospectus records niobium bought from CBMM to meet ITER's requirements.
notes.traceability: One industrial mine and a named distributor (CITIC Metal): the route is visible end to end.
notes.leverage: Superconductor niobium is a sliver of a market dominated by steelmaking.

notes.harm: 21 workers killed in a 2023 smelter blast; coercive land-taking with police and military; rising respiratory illness.
notes.evidence: Sayari shows no path from Hastelloy substrate to Indonesian nickel.
notes.traceability: Nickel from many origins is melted together in alloy mills; Chinese mills have no upstream data.
notes.leverage: Hastelloy mills serve the chemical industry; tape substrate is a tiny share.

notes.harm: Tailings damage to rivers and killings linked to security forces reported; seven workers died in a 2025 mine disaster.
notes.evidence: CFS's copper conductor came from Luvata Pori, which buys Indonesian cathode; the cathode-to-conductor link is not batch-traced.
notes.traceability: Cathode carries its smelter of origin, but mixes with other supply at the conductor maker.
notes.leverage: Fusion is a negligible share of world copper demand.

notes.harm: Armed-group control and extortion at some Colombian mines (2 sources); no documented forced labour or killings at these mines.
notes.evidence: A Western powder maker buys through a trader that also handles Rwandan ore; no shipment shows conflict ore reaching it.
notes.traceability: Concentrate from many origins is converted to APT and powder.
notes.leverage: Fusion buys from a handful of qualified makers (e.g. A.L.M.T.), which could pass sourcing conditions upstream.

notes.harm: Residents' pollution complaints led to a 2016 government inspection; no documented abuses against workers.
notes.evidence: Sayari shows A.L.M.T. taking tungsten APT only from Masan at Nui Phao (2023–26); which batches went to ITER is not recorded.
notes.traceability: One mine-to-processor complex feeds one maker, so origin survives further than in most chains.
notes.leverage: A.L.M.T. is one of very few fusion-grade suppliers; ITER and F4E are significant customers of its fusion line.

notes.harm: Chronic beryllium disease among workers is documented (settlements; a 2023 federal claim from the Utah mill).
notes.evidence: Materion has a public supply agreement with Commonwealth Fusion Systems.
notes.traceability: A single US mine and mill: origin is clear.
notes.leverage: Fusion is a new but visible customer of a small specialist supplier.

notes.harm: Human Rights Watch documents police and company violence against protesters at a Limpopo chrome mine.
notes.evidence: No record links this chrome to the mills that made ITER's or EUROFER97 steel.
notes.traceability: Chrome is alloyed into steel at the mill; origin is not tracked.
notes.leverage: Fusion's steel demand is tiny next to the stainless steel industry.

status: Scores are a first judgement from the evidence on this site, pending the author's review.
